settings.label: Server address
settings.description: The public address users reach the site at; every link and callback the server builds starts with it. Sign-in callbacks, links in emails and Telegram replies, payment callbacks, generated image links and the docs examples use it, and the CSRF check accepts requests from its origin. Enter the scheme and host as users type them; a trailing slash is removed on save. The default http://localhost:3000 only works on the server itself. Passkeys are bound to its host name: after a move to another domain, users register their passkeys again.

examples.effect: Password reset emails link to https://api.example.com/user/reset and an OIDC provider calls back to https://api.example.com/oauth/oidc/<slug>.

settings.label: Site name
settings.description: The site's name in page titles, the console header and emails. It also names the site in payment descriptions, authenticator apps, passkey prompts and notification webhooks. Empty shows Modeltaps.

settings.label: Logo URL
settings.description: The image at the top of every email and on the signed-out and device authorization pages. Use an absolute https address so mail clients can load it. Empty shows the built-in mark on those pages and no image in emails.

examples.effect: Emails show the logo 130 px wide above the text; the signed-out page shows it instead of the built-in mark.

settings.label: Home page content
settings.description: Your own home page in place of the built-in one. A value starting with http:// or https:// is shown in a full-page frame; anything else is rendered as Markdown, or as sanitized HTML when it starts with a tag. Empty keeps the built-in home page.

examples.effect: The home page shows your marketing site in a full-page frame under the site header.

examples.value:
# Welcome
Sign in to get an API key.
examples.effect: The home page shows a heading and one line of text.

settings.label: About page
settings.description: The content of the About page. A value starting with http:// or https:// is shown in a full-page frame; anything else is rendered as Markdown, or as sanitized HTML when it starts with a tag. Empty shows the built-in About text with a link to the project.

examples.value: Example AI is run by Example Inc. Contact: support@example.com
examples.effect: The About page shows these two sentences.

settings.label: Footer
settings.description: HTML that replaces the footer of the public pages. It is sanitized before display. Empty shows the default footer with the copyright and the docs link. A custom footer also makes the home page render in the console app instead of the prebuilt static page.

examples.effect: Every public page ends with this line instead of the default footer.

settings.label: Analytics code
settings.description: HTML added to the head of every page, for analytics scripts such as Google Analytics, Umami or Plausible. It runs for every visitor with full access to the page, so paste only code from a provider you trust. Empty adds nothing.

examples.effect: Umami counts the page views of the console and the public pages.

settings.label: Sync the icon library
settings.description: Keeps the vendor and channel icon library up to date from the npm registry, checked every 24 hours. A newer version is used once it is verified; a failed check keeps the current icons. Off keeps the icons embedded in this build. Every node syncs on its own; browsers always load icons from this site.

settings.label: Icon library registry
settings.description: The npm registry the icon library sync downloads from. Enter an http or https address without a query; a trailing slash is removed. Empty uses https://registry.npmmirror.com.

examples.effect: Downloads the icon library from the official npm registry.
The default mirror, quicker to reach from mainland China.

settings.label: Fetch icons for unknown vendors
settings.description: When a vendor or channel without a built-in icon is saved, the server fetches its website's favicon and caches it. Browsers still load every icon from this site. Off leaves those vendors without a fetched icon.

settings.label: Show amounts in US dollars
settings.description: Shows balances, quotas and costs as US dollar amounts in the console, the logs and the billing API. Each amount is quota / quota per dollar. Off shows raw quota numbers. Only the display changes, not what is charged.

examples.effect: With the default 500000 quota per dollar, a balance of 1,000,000 quota shows as $2.00.
The same balance shows as 1,000,000.

settings.label: Report API key quota in the billing API
settings.description: The billing API reports the calling API key's quota instead of the user's balance. This covers the OpenAI-style endpoints /v1/dashboard/billing/subscription and /usage. A key with unlimited quota still reports the user's balance, and organization keys always report their own quota. Off always reports the user's balance.

settings.label: Quota per dollar
settings.description: How many quota units make one US dollar; every conversion between quota and dollars uses it. A top-up of $1 credits this much quota, and dollar amounts in the console, logs and billing API are quota divided by it. Balances are stored in quota, so changing it on a running site changes what every balance is worth: keep 500000 unless the site is new.

examples.effect: The default: a $10 top-up credits 5,000,000 quota, and 1,000 quota is $0.002.
On a running site, a stored balance of 5,000,000 quota drops from $10 to $5.

settings.label: Default language
settings.description: The language emails and the home page use when a person's language is unknown. Users who picked a language in the console get emails in theirs; the home page uses it when the browser's language is not supported. The email template editor opens on it. Empty means English.

settings.label: Top-up link
settings.description: An outside shop where users buy redemption codes, opened in a new tab from the top-up page. Empty hides the button.

examples.effect: The top-up page shows a button under the redemption code field that opens the shop.

settings.label: Docs link
settings.description: Where the site's documentation lives, linked from the footer, the account menu and the API pages. /llms.txt and the agent skill file point to it too. Empty hides the external docs links; signed-in users still get the console's built-in docs.

examples.effect: Each API page links to its own page under https://docs.example.com.

settings.label: Announcement
settings.description: A banner at the top of the console for signed-in users, until each one reads or closes it. It shows again whenever the text changes. Markdown and HTML are supported. Empty shows no announcement.

examples.value: Maintenance on Saturday 02:00-03:00 UTC: requests may fail for a few minutes.
examples.effect: Every signed-in user sees the banner once; editing the text shows it to everyone again.

enum.label: Built-in accounts
enum.description: This site manages users, passwords, email codes and passkeys, optionally with GitHub, WeChat and other third-party sign-in. No external service is needed.

enum.label: External identity provider
enum.description: An OIDC service handles sign-in, sign-up, phone numbers, two-step verification and third-party sign-in. This site shows no sign-in form of its own: /login goes straight to the provider.

settings.label: Account system
settings.description: Whether this site manages its own accounts or leaves them to an external identity provider. With an external provider, the site's password, email code, passkey and social sign-in switches stop applying to regular users; only root keeps the emergency sign-in at /login/admin. Switching to external needs an enabled identity provider marked as the site identity, and saving asks for confirmation either way.

settings.label: Password sign-in
settings.description: Users can sign in with their username or email and password. When off, regular users sign in with an email code, a passkey or a social account; root can still use its password to reach the console. Only applies with built-in accounts.

settings.label: Email code sign-in
settings.description: Users can sign in with a code sent to their verified email instead of a password. It needs a working mail service: without one the option is not offered on the sign-in page. Only applies with built-in accounts.

settings.label: Passkeys
settings.description: Users can add passkeys (fingerprint, face or a hardware key) on their security page and sign in with them. When off, passkeys can neither be added nor used. With an external identity provider only root can use them, for the emergency sign-in.

settings.label: New user sign-up
settings.description: Whether new accounts can be created at all. When off, nobody can sign up: not with a password, not on a first social or identity provider sign-in, and organizations cannot create member accounts. Existing users still sign in.

settings.label: Password sign-up
settings.description: New users can sign up with a username and password. When off, new accounts come only from social sign-in, and organizations cannot create member accounts. Needs New user sign-up on; only applies with built-in accounts.

settings.label: Email verification at sign-up
settings.description: Password sign-up asks for an email and the code sent to it, and the account keeps that email as verified. It needs a working mail service. Social sign-ups are not affected. With the email domain restriction on, codes only go to allowed domains.

settings.label: Invite code required to sign up
settings.description: New users must enter a valid invite code, both for password sign-up and for a first social sign-in. Invite codes are managed on the invite codes page. Existing users and member accounts created by organizations do not need one.

settings.label: Bot check
settings.description: Cloudflare Turnstile checks that a person is behind sign-in, sign-up, password reset and the emails with codes. It cannot be turned on before the Turnstile site key is saved, and it needs the secret key too. A passed check covers the session for 10 minutes by default.

settings.label: Admin emergency sign-in
settings.description: Keeps /login/admin open so root can sign in with its password or passkey when the identity provider is down. Only root gets through; account lockout, rate limits and the bot check still apply. It exists only with an external identity provider. When off, nobody can reach the console while the provider is down.

settings.label: GitHub sign-in
settings.description: Users can sign in and sign up with their GitHub account. It cannot be turned on before the GitHub client ID is saved. Only applies with built-in accounts.

settings.label: GitHub client ID
settings.description: The client ID of the OAuth app you registered on GitHub. Register it with this site's address as the homepage URL and <server address>/oauth/github as the callback URL.

settings.label: GitHub client secret
settings.description: The client secret of the same GitHub OAuth app. It is never shown again after saving; leave the field empty to keep the stored one.

settings.label: Match GitHub accounts by ID only
settings.description: GitHub sign-in no longer matches old accounts by their GitHub login name, only by GitHub's numeric account ID. When off, an account from before IDs were stored is matched once by login name and then keeps the ID. A login name can be renamed and taken by someone else, so turn it on once old accounts have signed in.

settings.label: WeChat sign-in
settings.description: Users can sign in and sign up through your WeChat official account. They follow it, get a code and enter it on the sign-in page. It needs a WeChat login server and cannot be turned on before its address is saved. Only applies with built-in accounts.

settings.label: WeChat login server address
settings.description: The address of the WeChat login server behind your official account. The site asks it which WeChat user a code belongs to.

examples.effect: Codes are checked at https://wechat.example.com/api/wechat/user.

settings.label: WeChat login server token
settings.description: The access token the site sends to the WeChat login server with every check, as set on that server. It is never shown again after saving; leave the field empty to keep the stored one.

settings.label: Official account QR code
settings.description: A link to the QR code image of your WeChat official account. The WeChat sign-in dialog shows it so users can scan it, follow the account and get their code.

examples.effect: The sign-in dialog shows this image for users to scan.

settings.label: Lark sign-in
settings.description: Users can sign in and sign up with their Lark (Feishu) account. It uses the app whose App ID and App Secret you enter on this card. Only applies with built-in accounts.

settings.label: Lark App ID
settings.description: The App ID of the Lark (Feishu) app users sign in with. Create a web app on the Lark open platform and set its redirect URL to <server address>/oauth/lark.

settings.label: Lark App Secret
settings.description: The App Secret of the same Lark app. It is never shown again after saving; leave the field empty to keep the stored one.

settings.label: LINUX DO sign-in
settings.description: Users can sign in and sign up with their LINUX DO account. It cannot be turned on before the client ID and client secret are saved. Only applies with built-in accounts.

settings.label: LINUX DO client ID
settings.description: The client ID of the OAuth app you registered on LINUX DO, with <server address>/oauth/linuxdo as its callback URL.

settings.label: LINUX DO client secret
settings.description: The client secret of the same LINUX DO OAuth app. It is never shown again after saving; leave the field empty to keep the stored one.

settings.label: Minimum trust level
settings.description: LINUX DO accounts below the minimum trust level cannot sign up or be linked. Whether existing users are checked too is up to the dynamic limit. It needs LINUX DO sign-in on.

settings.label: Lowest LINUX DO trust level
settings.description: The lowest LINUX DO trust level allowed in, from 1 to 4: 1 basic, 2 member, 3 regular, 4 leader. Only applies while the minimum trust level is on.

examples.effect: Every account from basic users up gets in: only brand-new level 0 accounts are refused.
Members (level 2) and above get in; basic users (level 1) are refused.
Only regular users (level 3) and leaders (level 4) get in.

settings.label: Check existing users too
settings.description: The minimum trust level is checked on every LINUX DO sign-in, also for existing users. An existing user whose level is now too low is refused. When off, only new sign-ups are checked. It needs the minimum trust level on.

settings.label: Turnstile site key
settings.description: The site key of the widget you created in the Cloudflare Turnstile dashboard. The sign-in and sign-up pages load the check with it. The invisible widget type disturbs users least.

settings.label: Turnstile secret key
settings.description: The secret key of the same Turnstile widget; the server uses it to confirm each check with Cloudflare. It is never shown again after saving; leave the field empty to keep the stored one.

settings.label: Email domain restriction
settings.description: Sign-up verification codes only go to emails on the allowed domains, which keeps out throwaway mailboxes. Organizations cannot create member accounts with other emails either. It only stops password sign-up while email verification is on, and it cannot be turned on with an empty domain list.

settings.label: Allowed email domains
settings.description: The email domains allowed while the restriction is on, one per line (stored comma-separated). A domain matches exactly: example.com does not allow mail.example.com.

examples.effect: alice@gmail.com and bob@outlook.com get codes; carol@tempmail.dev is refused.
Only company addresses like alice@example.com can sign up; alice@mail.example.com cannot.

settings.label: New user quota
settings.description: The quota a new account starts with, granted once when it is created and logged as a sign-up bonus. In quota units: 500,000 = $1 at the default quota per unit; the field also takes dollars. Accounts an organization creates for its members start at 0, and changing it leaves existing balances alone. 0 gives new users nothing until they top up or redeem a code.

examples.effect: $2 of trial credit: about 119,000 output tokens of a $15 per million model sold at ratio 1.12.
New users can call nothing until they top up or redeem a code.

settings.label: Fixed pre-charge
settings.description: A fixed amount added to the up-front reservation of every token-priced request, on top of its estimated cost. The reservation (estimated input + reserved output tokens + this) is held from the balance or the API key's quota while the request runs and settled to the real cost when it ends, so it decides who may start a request, never what is charged. A balance below the reservation is refused with insufficient quota. In quota units: 500 = $0.001. Requests priced per call or per minute reserve their own price instead.

examples.effect: The default. A request with 2,000 input tokens on a $3 / $15 per million model at ratio 1.12 holds 3,360 + 34,406 + 500 = 38,266 quota (about $0.077) until it settles.
Every request needs $0.10 more than its estimate to start, so nearly empty balances are refused earlier.
Only the estimate is held: a balance just above it can still start a request.

settings.label: Reserved output tokens
settings.description: How many output tokens a token-priced request reserves up front, or the request's own max_tokens when smaller. Reserving its likely output keeps concurrent requests from driving a balance far below zero; the charge is settled to the real usage when the request ends. 0 reserves no output, only the input estimate and the fixed pre-charge.

examples.effect: The default. A $15 per million output model at ratio 1.12 reserves 4,096 x 8.4 = 34,406 quota (about $0.069) per request; a request with max_tokens 1,000 reserves 8,400.
Long reasoning answers are covered up front: 32,000 x 8.4 = 268,800 quota (about $0.54) on the same model, so a balance below that cannot start a request.

settings.label: Quota warning emails
settings.description: Email users when their balance falls below the warning threshold, and again when it runs out. Each email is sent once; another goes out only after the balance has clearly recovered and fallen again. Needs a mail service. Users can turn the emails off or set their own threshold in their personal settings; organization API keys never send them. When off nobody gets them, and settlement skips the balance read the check needs.

settings.label: Warning threshold
settings.description: The balance below which a user gets the "running low" email, in quota units (500,000 = $1). It is the default for users who have not set their own threshold. After an email the next one waits until the balance has gone back above the threshold plus 10% of it (or plus the fixed pre-charge, if larger) and fallen again. 0 sends only the "used up" email.

examples.effect: The default: the email goes out when $0.002 is left, about when the balance runs out.
Users hear when less than $10 is left; the next email comes only after the balance went back above $11 and fell again.

settings.label: Payment cost
settings.description: What taking a payment costs the site, as a percentage of the amount: card fees and currency conversion. Nobody is charged it. It only lowers the revenue the price check and the margin figures compare channel costs with: net revenue = catalog price x the default group's ratio x (1 - payment cost). 0 counts payments as free.

examples.effect: Card fee 3% plus 1% for currency conversion. With the default group at 1.12, $1 of catalog price brings in 1.12 x 0.96 = $1.0752.
Payments cost nothing: the price check compares channel costs with the full price.

settings.label: Charge empty replies
settings.description: Charge token-priced requests whose reply has no output tokens for their input. When off such requests are free, although the upstream may still bill you for the input. Requests priced per call or per minute are charged either way, and a request with no tokens at all is never charged.

examples.effect: An empty reply to 10,000 input tokens of a $3 per million model costs the user $0.03 at ratio 1.
The same request is free for the user; you still pay the upstream for the input.

settings.label: Approximate token counting
settings.description: Count tokens locally as 0.38 tokens per byte of text instead of running the model's tokenizer. Local counts are used for the up-front reservation and when an upstream reply carries no usage; replies that report their usage are billed by it. It saves CPU on busy instances at the cost of accuracy, worst for text outside the Latin alphabet.

examples.effect: 1,000 characters of English (1,000 bytes) count as 380 tokens; 1,000 Chinese characters (3,000 bytes) count as 1,140.

enum.label: Write increases, hold decreases
enum.description: A price that went up is written at once, so you never sell below a new cost; a decrease waits for your review.

enum.label: Write every change
enum.description: The price table follows the upstream price lists both ways.

enum.label: New models only
enum.description: Every change to an existing price waits for your review.

settings.label: Automatic price sync
settings.description: What the automatic price syncs (at startup, daily and when a channel is saved) write for models that already have a price. New models are always added and locked prices never change. Changes that are not written, and locked prices below the upstream price, are sent as notifications; review and apply them from the channel's price sync.

examples.effect: An upstream raises a model's output from $10 to $12 per million: written at once. It cuts it to $8: the table keeps $10 and you are notified.
Both changes wait in the notification until you apply them.

settings.label: Reset time zone
settings.description: The time zone whose midnight starts each daily, weekly and monthly limit period. It applies to API key period limits, organization budgets and member budgets. An IANA name; empty or unknown names fall back to UTC. Changing it moves the boundary of the current period.

examples.effect: The default: daily limits reset at 00:00 UTC, which is 08:00 in Beijing.
Daily limits reset at 00:00 Beijing time, which is 16:00 UTC the day before.
Limits reset at local midnight through daylight saving time: 05:00 UTC in winter, 04:00 UTC in summer.

settings.label: Week starts on
settings.description: The day weekly limit periods start, at midnight in the reset time zone. Daily and monthly periods are not affected.

examples.effect: A weekly API key limit used up on Saturday is available again on Monday at 00:00.
The same limit comes back on Sunday at 00:00.

settings.label: Invite rewards
settings.description: Pay invite rewards: sign-up bonuses for the inviter and the invitee, and the inviter's rebate on the first top-up. When off none are paid and the site hides its invite entries; who invited whom is still recorded.

settings.label: Inviter sign-up bonus
settings.description: The quota an inviter gets each time someone signs up with their invite link or code. In quota units (500,000 = $1). 0 pays nothing at sign-up; the first top-up rebate is set separately.

examples.effect: Each invited sign-up earns the inviter $2, whether or not the new user ever pays.
Inviters earn only the first top-up rebate, so fake sign-ups bring nothing.

settings.label: Invitee sign-up bonus
settings.description: Extra quota a new user gets for signing up with an invite link or code, on top of the new user quota. In quota units (500,000 = $1). 0 gives invited users only the new user quota.

examples.effect: With the new user quota at 1,000,000 ($2), an invited user starts with $3.

enum.label: Fixed
enum.description: The rebate is a quota amount, whatever the top-up.

enum.label: Percentage
enum.description: The rebate is a percentage of the quota the top-up bought.

settings.label: First top-up rebate type
settings.description: How the inviter's rebate on an invited user's first paid top-up is counted: a fixed quota or a percentage of the top-up. The first top-up rebate sets the amount.

settings.label: First top-up rebate
settings.description: What an inviter earns when someone they invited makes a first paid top-up. For the fixed type it is quota units (500,000 = $1); for the percentage type a whole percentage from 0 to 100 of the quota bought. Only the first paid top-up earns it: later top-ups and redemption codes earn nothing. 0 turns the rebate off.

examples.effect: Percentage: an invited user's first $50 top-up (25,000,000 quota) earns the inviter 2,500,000 quota, $5.
Fixed: the inviter gets $2 for the first top-up, whether it is $1 or $500.

settings.label: CNY collection rate
settings.description: How many yuan one US dollar of top-up costs at gateways that charge in CNY. A top-up of $X costs X x this rate there, times the gateway's own rate, plus its fee. It changes neither balances nor the quota a top-up buys, and USD gateways ignore it. Use the real exchange rate; for promotions use top-up discounts or a gateway's rate.

examples.effect: A $100 top-up costs ¥730 at a CNY gateway and $100 at a USD gateway; both buy 50,000,000 quota.
The same top-up costs ¥710: you take ¥20 less for the same quota.

settings.label: Minimum top-up
settings.description: The smallest top-up a user or an organization can pay, in whole US dollars. Smaller amounts are refused before a payment is created. 0 and 1 both allow any amount from $1.

examples.effect: Users can top up any whole amount from $1 (500,000 quota).
A $5 top-up is refused; $10 is the least, buying 5,000,000 quota.

settings.label: Payment callback address
settings.description: The address payment gateways send their payment notices to, when it differs from the server address. Empty uses the gateway's own callback domain, then the server address. Notices go to <address>/api/payment/notify/<gateway id> (EPay: <address>/api/user/epay/notify), which must be reachable from the internet, or paid orders are never credited.

examples.effect: Gateways call https://pay.example.com/api/payment/notify/<gateway id> while users keep using the main domain.

settings.label: Top-up discounts
settings.description: Discounts for fixed top-up amounts: a JSON object from a whole-dollar amount to the share of the price the user pays. Only those exact amounts are discounted; others pay full price. The quota is never discounted: $100 always buys 100 x 500,000 quota at the default quota per unit. A gateway's percentage fee is charged on the discounted price. Empty means no discounts.

examples.effect: A $100 top-up costs $95 (¥693.50 at a CNY rate of 7.3) and buys 50,000,000 quota; $99 or $101 pay full price.
$50 costs $49 and $200 costs $180; every other amount pays full price.

enum.label: Call order
enum.description: Supplies are tried in the call order of the Providers page; cost does not move them.

enum.label: Cheaper first
enum.description: Supplies that are clearly cheaper and serve well take a model's requests ahead of the call order.

settings.label: Order by
settings.description: Whether a supply's cost (its channel's list price with the channel's fee) moves it ahead of the call order. Users pay the catalog price times their group ratio either way; only your cost changes. With cheaper first, a supply must be cheaper by the minimum saving and reach the minimum success rate to be put ahead; closer costs keep the call order and share a tier by weight, and supplies of unknown cost come last.

examples.effect: Requesty (cost x1.05) and the official API (x1.00) at the same priority with weights 3 and 1 take about 75% and 25% of gpt-5.1's requests.
A relay at x0.80 takes gpt-5.1's requests from Requesty at a higher priority while it succeeds 95% of the time; when it drops below, Requesty takes them back.

settings.label: Minimum saving
settings.description: With cost first, how much cheaper a supply must be than another to take requests ahead of it, as a percentage of the dearer cost. Supplies closer than that count as the same cost and share requests by priority and weight, so a slightly cheaper supply does not take all of a model's traffic. 0 puts any supply that is cheaper by more than 0.1% ahead.

examples.effect: OpenRouter (fee 5.5%) and Requesty (fee 5%) count as the same cost; a relay at x0.90 is put ahead of both.
Requesty (x1.05) is put ahead of OpenRouter (x1.055).

settings.label: Minimum success rate
settings.description: With cost first, the success rate a supply needs over the current and the previous hour to be put ahead for its cost. A cheaper supply below it is ordered as if its cost were unknown, behind the supplies that serve well, until its rate recovers. A supply with fewer than 20 attempts in that time is not judged. 0 turns the check off. It is also the uptime over the last day a host of a Vercel AI Gateway model needs to be in the order of hosts the channel asks for, whichever cost order is set.

examples.effect: A discount reseller that failed 12 of its last 100 requests stops taking requests first; the next healthy supply takes them.
The cheapest supply always leads, however often it fails; only pauses keep it out.

settings.label: Route by supplies
settings.description: Requests are routed through each public model's supplies instead of the channels' model lists and model mappings. Turning it on first turns the channels' models and model mappings into supplies (only what is still missing), so every model a channel serves keeps working. While on, requests are billed by the public model, only published models are listed, the providers page orders the channels, and the call order, the order-by setting, intake rules and pause rules decide where a request goes. New installations start with it on. Turning it off goes back to the channels' model lists at once and keeps the supplies.

examples.effect: Requests follow each channel's models and model mapping; the supply pages only preview what would change.
A request for claude-sonnet-4-5 goes to the supplies of that public model, ordered by priority and cost.

settings.label: Intake rules for new upstream models
settings.description: What happens to a model a channel's upstream starts listing, for channels that add new upstream models on their own. It is a JSON array tried from the top, and the first rule whose conditions all hold decides; a model no rule matches waits for review. Conditions: endpoints (abilities such as chat, responses, images, any of them), vendors (vendor ids), families and patterns (globs such as claude-* or *-preview*), supplied (whether another channel already supplies it). action is enable (routes at once), pending (added switched off until an admin confirms), disable (added switched off) or skip (not added). placement is auto (last when others already supply it), policy (where the allocation policy puts it) or last. Empty uses the built-in rules; saved rules replace them as a whole, and a channel can use rules of its own.

examples.effect: The built-in rules: gpt-5-preview waits for review, a new chat model routes at once (behind the channels that already supply it), an image model waits for review.
A new Claude model routes at once after the model's other supplies; any other new model is not added and stays in the list of new upstream models.

settings.label: Keep each session on one channel
settings.description: Requests of one client session go to the channel that served it first, so the upstream prompt cache keeps hitting. A session is recognised by the Claude Code session in metadata.user_id, a session header such as Codex's session_id, the OpenAI prompt_cache_key, or else the same system prompt and first user message. Claude Code, Gemini CLI and Codex account channels are always sticky, whatever this says. When off, each request is routed on its own.

settings.label: Do not move a session on failure
settings.description: When a session's channel fails, the caller gets the error instead of a retry on another channel. The channel is not paused for that model either (channel-wide pauses still apply). Moving loses the upstream prompt cache and the conversation state Codex keeps upstream. Errors that say the channel can no longer serve (a rejected key, an empty balance) still move the session. Leave it off to favour availability.

settings.label: Session lifetime
settings.description: How long a session stays bound to its channel after its last request; every request starts the time again. Account channels (Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Codex) always keep 1 hour. 0 uses 1 hour as well.

examples.effect: A coding session paused for 50 minutes comes back to the same channel; after 70 minutes it may land elsewhere.
Matches the upstream's 5-minute prompt cache: past that the cache is gone, so the session is free to move.

settings.label: Charge the decision call
settings.description: Bills the call an auto routing policy makes to pick a model to the caller, at the decision model's price. It is charged once per session, as a log entry of its own. When off, the decision still runs, but the site pays for it and no consume log is written.

settings.label: Own routing policies
settings.description: Users and organizations can create routing policies of their own, called as policy/<name>. Users create personal policies under Routing policies in the workbench, organization owners and admins organization policies; an own policy overrides a platform policy of the same name for its own keys. When off, own policies are kept but no longer apply, and only platform policies resolve.

settings.label: Policies per user
settings.description: How many personal routing policies one user can create. Policies a user already has are kept when the cap is lowered; only new ones are refused. 0 sets no limit.

examples.effect: A user with 20 policies gets an error when creating the 21st.
Users can create as many policies as they like.

settings.label: Policies per organization
settings.description: How many routing policies one organization can create. Policies it already has are kept when the cap is lowered; only new ones are refused. 0 sets no limit.

examples.effect: An organization with 20 policies gets an error when creating the 21st.
Keeps organization policies few enough to review by hand.

settings.label: Retries
settings.description: How many other channels a failed request is tried on before the caller gets the error. Rate limits, upstream 5xx errors, rejected keys and exhausted balances are retried; invalid requests (most 400s), 408 timeouts, the gateway's own errors and requests pinned to one channel are not. The retries never exceed the channels that serve the model and stop once the retry time limit has passed. 0 returns the first failure.

examples.effect: A request to a model served by 5 channels is tried on at most 3 of them (the first plus 2 retries).
With only 2 channels serving the model, the request is tried on both and then fails: retries stop when no untried channel is left.
No retry: the first failure is returned to the caller.

settings.label: Rate limit cooldown
settings.description: How long a channel is kept away from a model after it answers that model with a 429 rate limit. While it cools down, new requests for the model go to other channels; its other models are not affected. When the upstream says when the limit resets, that time is used instead. It is the pause of the built-in rate_limit rule; custom rules carry their own seconds. 0 only skips the channel for the failed request.

examples.effect: After a 429 for gpt-4o, that channel takes no gpt-4o requests for 5 seconds; it keeps serving its other models.
A channel with a per-minute limit sits out the rest of the minute instead of collecting more 429s.
No cooldown: the next request may land on the same channel and hit the limit again.

settings.label: Retry time limit
settings.description: No new retry starts once this many seconds have passed since the request arrived. It is checked before each retry and does not cut an attempt that is already running, so long generations still finish. When it stops the retries, the caller gets a 503 saying the upstream is at capacity. 0 starts no retry at all.

examples.effect: A first channel that fails after 12 seconds is not retried; one that fails after 3 seconds is, as long as the 10 seconds are not used up.
Suits long reasoning requests: a channel failing after a minute still leaves room for another try.

settings.label: Per-status cooldown
settings.description: Cooldowns in seconds for other HTTP status codes, as a JSON object of status code and seconds. Like the rate limit cooldown it keeps the channel away from that one model. The built-in per_status rule applies it after the quota, credential, rate limit and model-not-found rules, so a 429 entry is never reached, and a listed 5xx code no longer waits for three failures in a minute. A code set to 0 is never cooled. Codes must be 100-599 and seconds whole numbers of 0 or more; empty adds none.

examples.effect: A channel answering a model with 503 takes no requests for it for 2 minutes, from the first 503 on.
502 cools the model on that channel for 1 minute, 504 for 5 minutes.
A 500 never pauses or cools the channel: the request moves on and the next one may use it again.

settings.label: Model not found pause
settings.description: How long a channel is kept away from a model after its upstream says the model does not exist. There is no field for it on this page: change it through the option API (PUT /api/option/). It covers errors such as "model not found", "does not exist" or "no endpoints found", but not when a 429 was seen in the same request. It is the pause of the built-in model_not_found rule, which also notifies admins; custom rules carry their own seconds. 0 never pauses for it.

examples.effect: A channel that lost access to gpt-4.5 stays out of gpt-4.5 requests for 6 hours, then gets tried again.
A model that was only briefly missing upstream comes back after 10 minutes.
The channel stays in rotation and keeps failing requests for the model until it is removed from the channel.

settings.label: Custom pause rules
settings.description: A JSON array of pause rules that replaces the built-in rules as a whole; empty uses the built-in ones. Rules are tried in order and the first match decides, after the channel's own rules. A rule matches on any of status_codes, keywords (substrings of the error, "re:" for a regular expression), error_types or error_codes, plus the flags unusable, model_not_found, rate_limit_reset and per_status_config; times and window_seconds make it count matches first. action is "pause" (for seconds, on the whole channel or, by default, the model) or "retry" (move on without pausing). probe sends a test request before resuming and doubles the pause when it fails; notify tells admins. Pauses under a minute are kept in memory only. Saved rules carry their own seconds, so the rate limit and model-not-found settings no longer apply to them.

examples.effect: A 402 or a low-balance message pauses the whole channel for 30 minutes and notifies admins; a test request runs before it resumes, and a balance refresh that finds money ends the pause early.
Two 529s for one model on one channel within a minute pause that model there for 5 minutes; if the test before resuming fails, the next pause lasts 10 minutes.
No rule: nothing is ever paused, a failing channel is only skipped for the request that failed.

settings.label: Disable channels that can no longer serve
settings.description: Disables a channel whose upstream says it can no longer serve, such as a rejected key or an empty balance. An exhausted quota, a disabled account or a disable keyword in the error count too. It applies to channel tests: on live requests such errors pause the channel through the pause rules instead. A disabled channel comes back only through a passing test with automatic recovery on, or by hand.

settings.label: Re-enable channels that pass a test
settings.description: A channel that was disabled automatically is enabled again when it passes a channel test. The test is a test of all channels, scheduled or started by hand, and must answer within the maximum response time. Channels an admin disabled are never enabled again on their own. When off, every disabled channel waits for an admin.

settings.label: Maximum response time
settings.description: A channel test slower than this many seconds disables an enabled channel and keeps a disabled one off. It applies to tests of all channels (scheduled in the All channels mode, or started from the channels page), whether or not automatic disabling is on; live requests are never timed against it. 0 sets no limit.

examples.effect: A channel that takes 7.3 seconds to answer the test request is disabled; one that answers in 2 seconds keeps serving.
Leaves slow reasoning models alone and only disables channels that hang.
Tests disable channels for errors only, never for slowness.

settings.label: Disable keywords
settings.description: Error messages, one per line, that mark a channel as unable to serve when an upstream error contains one. Matching is case-sensitive, so copy the upstream text exactly; a keyword wins over the built-in exceptions. A match moves the request to another channel and pauses the channel through the built-in credential rule (1 hour, tested before resuming); in a channel test it disables the channel when automatic disabling is on. Empty leaves only the built-in checks of status codes and known messages.

examples.effect: An upstream error containing this text pauses the whole channel for an hour instead of failing request after request.

examples.value: Your credit balance is too low
examples.effect: Also matched by the built-in quota rule, which comes first: the channel pauses for 30 minutes and resumes early once a balance refresh finds money.

enum.label: Auto-disabled channels only
enum.description: Tests only channels that were disabled automatically and, with automatic recovery on, enables those that pass; healthy channels spend nothing.

enum.label: All channels
enum.description: Tests every channel not disabled by hand: too slow ones are disabled, failing ones too when automatic disabling is on, and auto-disabled ones that pass come back.

enum.label: Off
enum.description: No scheduled test: disabled channels stay off until an admin tests or enables them.

settings.label: Scheduled channel test
settings.description: Which channels the gateway tests on its own, every test interval. Each test is one small request to the channel's test model and is billed by the upstream. The CHANNEL_TEST_FREQUENCY environment variable, when set, overrides this: all channels every that many minutes.

settings.label: Test interval
settings.description: Minutes between two scheduled channel tests, at least one. A new interval applies from the next round, without a restart. Shorter intervals bring channels back sooner but send more test requests.

examples.effect: An auto-disabled channel whose upstream recovered is back within about 10 minutes.
With All channels and 20 channels, 480 test requests a day.

settings.label: Account credential refresh
settings.description: How often the OAuth credentials of Codex, Claude Code, Gemini CLI and Antigravity channels are checked. Credentials expiring before the next check (plus 15 minutes) are refreshed even on idle or auto-disabled channels, so they do not fail on their first request after a quiet night; channels disabled by hand are skipped. A channel whose refresh starts failing sends one channel credential notice. 0 turns the background refresh off.

examples.effect: Every 30 minutes, tokens that expire within the next 45 minutes are renewed in the background.
No background refresh: a token can expire while its channel is idle.

settings.label: Hide upstream errors
settings.description: Callers get a generic error instead of the upstream's own text, which may name the provider or show parts of a key. Upstream errors other than 400 become a 503 with the unified message (a 429 stays a 429 so clients back off), rejected channel keys get a fixed message, and a missing model a 404. 400 errors pass through, since they are about the request. Turn it off only for a while, to see what the upstream really says.

settings.label: Unified error message
settings.description: The message callers get when an upstream fails and upstream errors are hidden. The request id is added to it so a caller can quote it. Empty uses "Upstream for the current group is at capacity, please try again later". It has no effect while upstream errors are shown.

examples.value: Service busy, please retry in a minute
examples.effect: A failed request answers 503 with "Service busy, please retry in a minute (request id: ...)".

settings.label: Ignore case in model names
settings.description: The model name a caller sends matches channels and prices whatever its case. When on, GPT-4o finds the channels and the price of gpt-4o, including wildcard prices. When off, names must match exactly and a differently cased name gets no channel.

settings.label: Answer with the requested model name
settings.description: The model field of every response carries the name the caller asked for, not the upstream model it was mapped to. Some clients check that the reply names the model they requested. When off, it is done only for channels and supplies that switch it on themselves.

examples.effect: A request for my-chat mapped to gpt-4o-2024-08-06 answers with "model": "my-chat".
The same request answers with "model": "gpt-4o-2024-08-06", unless its channel or supply renames it.

settings.label: Claude Messages API
settings.description: Callers can use the Anthropic Messages format (/claude/v1/messages and the coding agent endpoints) besides the OpenAI format. Claude Code and the Anthropic SDKs need it. When off, those endpoints answer 403 and llms.txt no longer lists them.

settings.label: Gemini API
settings.description: Callers can use the Google Gemini format (the /gemini/v1beta endpoints, Live API included) besides the OpenAI format. Gemini CLI and the Google SDKs need it. When off, those endpoints answer 403.

settings.label: Add prompt cache markers
settings.description: Adds cache_control markers to requests for Anthropic models so the upstream caches the prompt. Later requests then read it at the cache price. It covers Claude, Opus, Sonnet and Haiku models on any channel type, and applies on channels whose prompt caching setting is Inherit; a channel set to On or Off decides for itself, along with the TTL and which messages are marked. Requests that already carry cache_control are left alone. An API key's prompt caching setting, or the X-Modeltaps-Prompt-Cache header, decides for its own requests. On by default.

examples.effect: A client that sends no cache markers still gets its long system prompt cached upstream for 5 minutes.
Only clients that mark their prompts themselves, and channels set to On, use the cache.

settings.label: Pass upstream responses through
settings.description: Keeps upstream responses as close to the original as possible. Non-streaming Claude and Bedrock responses are passed byte for byte, streams keep their model field, and upstream headers such as anthropic-ratelimit-*, x-ratelimit-* and x-amzn-* reach the caller. When off, responses are rebuilt like those of any other channel.

settings.label: Default thinking budget
settings.description: The share of max_tokens Claude may spend thinking when a request asks for thinking without its own budget. It applies to OpenAI-format requests sent to Claude. budget_tokens = max_tokens x this value, and never below 1024. A request that names an effort gets 0.2, 0.5 or 0.8 for low, medium and high instead.

examples.effect: With max_tokens 10000, Claude may think for 8000 tokens and has 2000 left for the answer.
With max_tokens 4096, the thinking budget is 2048 tokens.
With max_tokens 8192, 819 would be too small, so the budget is raised to 1024.

settings.label: Default max tokens
settings.description: The max_tokens sent to Claude when an OpenAI-format or Responses request sets no output limit. Claude requires one, so it is a JSON object of model name and tokens, with "default" for every other model. Requests that set max_tokens or max_completion_tokens keep their own. Empty means {"default": 8192}; an object without "default" leaves unlisted models without a limit and Claude rejects them, and text that is not valid JSON is ignored.

examples.effect: Every Claude request without a limit may write up to 8192 tokens.
claude-sonnet-4-5 requests without a limit may write up to 64000 tokens, other models 8192.

settings.label: Show Gemini thoughts
settings.description: Gemini models whose responses include their thought summaries, as a JSON object of model name and true. It only applies to models that can think; unlisted models keep thoughts out unless the request asks for them. Empty lists none, and text that is not valid JSON is ignored.

examples.effect: gemini-2.5-pro replies carry the model's reasoning before the answer; gemini-2.5-flash replies do not.

settings.label: Max prompt tokens
settings.description: Requests to AWS Bedrock channels with more input tokens than this are refused before reaching the upstream. They get a 400 "prompt is too long", which Claude Code reads like Anthropic's own; Bedrock would otherwise hang on them until its timeout. A model's context length in the catalog takes precedence; other channel types are not checked. 0 turns the check off.

examples.effect: A 1.2 million token prompt to a Bedrock model with no context length in the catalog gets a 400 at once.
Prompts over 200000 tokens are refused for Bedrock models without a known context length.

settings.label: Run the inclusion rules
settings.description: Runs the inclusion rules after each daily model library sync, so new releases join the catalog on their own. Edited on the Models page, Inclusion rules tab. Off, the library still syncs but nothing is added or retired automatically.

settings.label: Apply the inclusion rules
settings.description: Lets the inclusion rules change the catalog: on, they add and retire models and notify admins of what they did. Off is a dry run: they change nothing and only notify admins of what they would do. Edited on the Models page, Inclusion rules tab.

examples.effect: A new Claude release is reported as "would be enabled"; the catalog stays as it is.
The same release joins the catalog enabled, and admins are told it was added.

settings.label: Inclusion rules
settings.description: The rules that decide which library models join the catalog and which catalog models are retired. They are saved as a JSON list and edited on the Models page, Inclusion rules tab. Rules are tried in order and the first one whose conditions all hold decides: enable, add disabled, leave out or retire. Conditions are labs, id patterns, release age, whether a channel can supply the model, deprecated, open weights and endpoints. Each model is decided once, so a model you remove is not added back. Empty uses the built-in rules; an empty list does nothing.

examples.effect: Deprecated catalog models stop being listed but stay callable; nothing is added.
An Anthropic model released in the last 60 days that a channel offers joins the catalog enabled.
The built-in rules: retire deprecated models, add previews disabled, enable recent models of the main labs, add other supplied models disabled.

settings.label: Consume logs
settings.description: Write a consume log for every charged request: user, API key, model, tokens, cost, channel and timing. When off no new records are written and charging goes on as before, but the log list, the usage statistics built from logs and per-user histories have a gap. Top-ups, sign-up bonuses and other system logs are written either way.

settings.label: Log failed requests
settings.description: Write an error log when a request still fails after its retries, with the error the client got and every channel tried. Requests refused locally (insufficient quota, invalid parameters) are not logged.

settings.label: Hourly channel metrics
settings.description: Count attempts, successes, latency, time to first token and output speed per channel, model and hour. The counters are kept in memory, written every minute and read through GET /api/channel/metrics. When off nothing new is counted; stored hours stay until they expire.

settings.label: Keep metrics for (days)
settings.description: How many days of hourly channel metrics are kept; older hours are deleted every night at 03:10 server time. 0 keeps them forever.

examples.effect: The default: at most 30 x 24 = 720 rows per channel and model.
Nothing is deleted: the table grows by one row per channel, model and hour in use.

settings.label: Delete old consume logs
settings.description: Delete consume logs older than the retention days every night at 03:00 server time, with their kept bodies. Error and system logs stay, and so do the daily usage statistics already built from the deleted logs.

settings.label: Keep consume logs for (days)
settings.description: How many days of consume logs are kept when old logs are deleted automatically. Older logs go in the nightly cleanup; 0 deletes nothing.

examples.effect: The default: a month of logs is kept; a log written on 1 May is gone by 1 June.
A quarter is kept, about three times the rows of the default.

settings.label: Allow keeping request bodies
settings.description: Site-wide switch for keeping the full request and response bodies of API calls, for troubleshooting. When off (the default, zero data retention) no API key keeps them and the option is hidden from personal and organization settings. When on, a personal account turns it on for its keys in the personal settings, and an organization's owners and admins choose: no key, every key, or the keys they select. Nothing is kept until then. Bodies are cut at 1 MB each by default, kept 30 days, and never include API keys or auth headers.

settings.label: Content safety check
settings.description: Check the text of every request with the safety tool before it goes to a channel, and refuse matches with a 400 error. Messages, system prompts, tool definitions and the client events of Realtime and Gemini Live sessions are checked; images and audio are not.

enum.label: Keyword
enum.description: Refuses requests whose text contains a word of the blocked keywords.

settings.label: Safety tool
settings.description: The tool that runs the content safety check. Keyword is the one built in. A tool that is not installed refuses every request.

settings.label: Blocked keywords
settings.description: The words the Keyword tool blocks, one per line. A request is refused when its text contains any of them, ignoring case, also inside longer words. Empty lines are ignored.

examples.effect: Refuses "Plan a casino night" and "best casinos".
Also refuses "class" and "password": short words match inside longer ones, so list whole, unusual words.

settings.label: Image download proxy
settings.description: An HTTP or SOCKS5 proxy for downloading the images that requests link to. The gateway fetches them to count their tokens and to pass them on as data, and without a proxy the image hosts see this server's IP. With a Cloudflare Worker set, the proxy only carries the call to the Worker. Empty downloads directly.

examples.effect: Image downloads go through the local SOCKS5 proxy on port 1080.
Image downloads go through an HTTP proxy in the private network.

settings.label: Cloudflare Worker image proxy
settings.description: A Cloudflare Worker that downloads the images requests link to, instead of this server. The gateway posts the image address and the Worker key to it and reads the image back, so the image hosts only see Cloudflare. It takes precedence over the image download proxy. Some image hosts refuse Cloudflare, and those images then fail. Empty uses no Worker.

examples.effect: Every image linked in a request is fetched by that Worker.

settings.label: Cloudflare Worker key
settings.description: The key sent to the Cloudflare Worker with every image download, for a Worker that checks one. Leave it empty when the Worker checks none or no Worker is set.

enum.label: This gateway
enum.description: Kept on this gateway for 1 hour under the server address, at most 5 downloads per link and 2 MB/s per download. Several nodes need Redis so every node can serve every link.

enum.label: S3 compatible
enum.description: AWS S3, Cloudflare R2, MinIO, Backblaze B2 and other S3 compatible storage. Without a public URL, links are signed for 1 hour and the bucket can stay private. The gateway deletes no files: add a lifecycle rule in the storage console (for example 1 day).

enum.label: Alibaba Cloud OSS
enum.description: Links are signed and valid for 1 hour, so the bucket can stay private.

enum.label: SM.MS
enum.description: Free image host; images are public.

enum.label: Imgur
enum.description: Free image host; images are public.

enum.label: Off
enum.description: Images come back as base64, and clients that only read the image URL get none.

settings.label: Image storage
settings.description: Where generated images are kept so a request that asks for an image URL gets a link. Gemini, Cloudflare Workers AI and Stability AI return image data only. Off answers with base64 instead: images endpoints give b64_json rather than url, and Gemini replies carry the whole image inline. A change applies at once on every node.

settings.label: Also store upstream image and video links
settings.description: Image and video links from upstreams are swapped for links on this site, which work where the upstream host is blocked. It covers image links from DALL·E, Flux and similar upstreams and from Midjourney tasks, and video links from Kling tasks. Images are fetched at once; a video is fetched on its first download and kept, up to 512 MB. A link that cannot be fetched is passed on as it is. When off, upstream links pass through.

settings.label: S3 endpoint
settings.description: The S3 API address of the storage, without the bucket. Without a public URL, links point at <endpoint>/<bucket>/... and are signed.

examples.effect: Cloudflare R2; the region is auto.
AWS S3 in Frankfurt; the region eu-central-1 is read from the address.

settings.label: S3 region
settings.description: The region requests are signed for; usually left empty. Empty reads it from AWS, Backblaze B2 and Wasabi endpoints and uses auto for anything else, which is what Cloudflare R2 expects.

examples.effect: Signs for us-east-1, for MinIO or another storage that expects a fixed region.

settings.label: S3 bucket
settings.description: The bucket images are uploaded to. It can stay private unless a public URL is set.

settings.label: S3 access key ID
settings.description: The ID of an access key that may write to the bucket; its secret goes in the next field.

settings.label: S3 access key secret
settings.description: The secret of the S3 access key. It is stored encrypted when an encryption key is set, never shown again, and saving the field empty keeps the stored one.

settings.label: S3 public URL
settings.description: A public address of the bucket or of a CDN in front of it; images then get plain public links under it. Empty gives links signed for 1 hour, and the bucket can stay private.

examples.effect: Images get links under https://img.example.com/ that work as long as the file exists.

settings.label: S3 Expires header
settings.description: Days written into the Expires header of each uploaded image, for caches and CDNs. It deletes nothing: use a lifecycle rule of the storage for that. 0 writes no header.

examples.effect: An image uploaded today says it expires tomorrow; the file stays until a lifecycle rule removes it.
No Expires header.

settings.label: OSS endpoint
settings.description: The endpoint of the Alibaba Cloud OSS region the bucket is in.

examples.effect: A bucket in Beijing; the region cn-beijing is read from the address.

settings.label: OSS region
settings.description: The OSS region the bucket is in; usually left empty. Empty reads it from an endpoint of the form oss-<region>.aliyuncs.com; other endpoints (an internal or accelerated one) need it, or uploads fail.

examples.effect: Signs for Hangzhou, for an endpoint the region cannot be read from.

settings.label: OSS bucket
settings.description: The OSS bucket images are uploaded to; it can stay private, since links are signed.

settings.label: OSS AccessKey ID
settings.description: The AccessKey ID of a RAM user that may write to the bucket; its secret goes in the next field.

settings.label: OSS AccessKey secret
settings.description: The AccessKey secret of the OSS user. It is stored encrypted when an encryption key is set, never shown again, and saving the field empty keeps the stored one.

settings.label: SM.MS API token
settings.description: The API token of your account on the free image host, used for uploads. Images there are public.

settings.label: Imgur client ID
settings.description: The client ID of an application registered with Imgur, used for anonymous uploads. Images there are public.

settings.label: Midjourney callbacks
settings.description: Passes the callback address (notifyHook) of a Midjourney task on to the upstream, which calls it when the task changes. The call comes from the upstream, not this site, so it carries the upstream's view of the task and tells the upstream the caller's address. When off, the address is dropped and callers poll the task status.

settings.label: Built-in chat
settings.description: Lets users try models in the console's playground and shows the quick-start chat on the dashboard. Off keeps the playground pages visible but disables running a request, and points users to the API docs instead. API keys and requests from other clients are not affected.

settings.label: Mail service preset
settings.description: Which preset the mail service in use was set up from, such as resend, ses, gmail or custom. It only shapes the console form; sending reads the server, port and account. Like every SMTP setting it mirrors the mail service in use and changes with it.

settings.label: SMTP server
settings.description: The host name of the SMTP server every email is sent through. It mirrors the mail service in use: add, edit or switch services on the Mail services card. Empty means the site cannot send mail, so login codes, password resets and quota warnings stop. When the deployment sets smtp.url (SMTP_URL), that wins and the console is read-only.

examples.effect: Mail goes out through Resend.

settings.label: SMTP port
settings.description: The port of the SMTP server: usually 465 for SSL/TLS and 587 for STARTTLS. With encryption Auto the port decides the encryption, and port 587 logs in with LOGIN instead of PLAIN. It mirrors the mail service in use.

examples.effect: With Auto, the connection is TLS from the first byte.
With Auto, the connection must upgrade with STARTTLS and logs in with LOGIN.
With Auto, STARTTLS is still required; pick STARTTLS if offered for a relay without TLS.

settings.label: SMTP username
settings.description: The user name the mail service logs in to the SMTP server with; for a mailbox it is the mailbox address. When no sender address is set, mail is sent from it. It mirrors the mail service in use.

settings.label: Sender address
settings.description: The address every email comes from. It must be an address the service lets you send from: one on a domain you verified with it, or the mailbox itself. It mirrors the mail service in use.

examples.effect: Users get mail from noreply@example.com; example.com must be verified with the service.

settings.label: Sender name
settings.description: The display name shown before the sender address. Empty shows the address alone. It mirrors the mail service in use.

examples.effect: Mail comes from Example AI <noreply@example.com>.

settings.label: Reply-to address
settings.description: Where replies to the site's emails go instead of the sender address. Empty sends replies to the sender address. It mirrors the mail service in use.

examples.effect: A user who replies to a login code email writes to support@example.com.

settings.label: SMTP password
settings.description: The password, app password or API key the mail service logs in with. It is never shown again after saving and is encrypted in the database when ENCRYPTION_KEY is set. It mirrors the mail service in use.

enum.label: Auto (by port)
enum.description: SSL/TLS on port 465, required STARTTLS on any other port.

enum.label: SSL/TLS
enum.description: TLS from the first byte, usually on port 465.

enum.label: STARTTLS (required)
enum.description: Upgrades to TLS after connecting; sending fails when the server cannot.

enum.label: STARTTLS if offered
enum.description: Upgrades when the server offers it, otherwise sends in plain text.

enum.label: None
enum.description: Plain text, for a relay on a trusted local network or for development.

settings.label: Encryption
settings.description: How the connection to the SMTP server is encrypted. Auto picks by port and suits almost every service. It mirrors the mail service in use.

settings.label: Email templates
settings.description: Your own subject and body for each email users get, per console language. The emails are the verification code, password reset, low balance and quota used up. Stored as JSON {"<template>": {"<language>": {"subject", "body"}}}; a template or language left out, or an empty subject or body, uses the built-in text of that language. Variables are a name in double curly braces, HTML-escaped in the body; the server adds the shared header with the logo and the footer. Unknown templates or languages are refused on save.

examples.effect: English verification emails get the new subject and keep the built-in body; every other email stays built-in.

settings.label: Turned-off notice kinds
settings.description: The kinds of admin notices that are not sent to any notice channel; the card's switches write it. Comma separated; empty sends every kind. The kinds are channel_disabled, channel_enabled, channel_test, low_balance, subscription_usage, price_change, price_source, model_drift, model_consistency, credential, supply_paused, supply_resumed, supply_failover, supply_above_quote and model_library. A notice channel can also take only some kinds.

examples.effect: Upstream price and model list changes are not sent; every other kind is.

settings.label: Notices per kind per hour
settings.description: The most notices of one kind sent in an hour; the rest are dropped. The hour starts with the first notice of the kind, and the first notice after a limited hour says how many were dropped. Each kind counts on its own, on each node. 0 means no limit.

examples.effect: The default: of 50 channel_disabled notices in one hour, 20 are sent; the next one after the hour says 30 were dropped.
Every notice is sent, however many.

settings.label: Subscription usage alert tiers
settings.description: The usage levels, in percent, at which a subscription channel (Codex, Claude Code) sends a notice for a usage window. Each tier fires once per window period and again after the window resets. Comma separated, each between 1 and 100; empty means 50, 75, 100 and 0 turns the alerts off. A channel's own tiers on its monitoring tab win over these. The notices are of the subscription_usage kind.

examples.effect: A 5-hour window at 82% sends one notice and at 96% another; after the reset both can fire again.
No usage alerts, except from channels with tiers of their own.

settings.label: Organizations
settings.description: Users can create and join organizations that share a balance, members, budgets and API keys. When off, users no longer see organizations and the organization API refuses every request; site admins still manage the existing ones, which are kept as they are.

settings.label: Personal balance transfer into organizations
settings.description: An organization's owner or admins can move their own personal balance into the organization's shared balance. The transfer is one-way: nothing moves back to a personal account. When off, transfers are refused.

settings.label: Organizations per user
settings.description: How many organizations one user can create. Organizations they only joined do not count, nor deleted ones. 0 means no limit.

examples.effect: A user who created 3 organizations must delete one before creating a fourth; joining others is not limited.
Each user runs at most one organization of their own.
Users create as many organizations as they like.

settings.label: Default member limit
settings.description: How many members an organization can have when a site admin has not set a limit for that organization. Changing it applies to every organization without a limit of its own, existing ones included. 0 means no limit.

examples.effect: An organization with 10 members cannot add an 11th until a site admin raises its limit.
Organizations without a limit of their own take any number of members.

enum.label: Return to the owner
enum.description: The remaining shared balance goes to the owner's personal account, with a log entry.

enum.label: Discard
enum.description: The remaining shared balance is cleared and returned to nobody.

settings.label: Balance of a deleted organization
settings.description: What happens to an organization's remaining shared balance when it is deleted, by its owner or a site admin. It has no field on the settings page and is only set through the option API (PUT /api/option/). Any value other than owner discards the balance.

settings.label: Priority
settings.description: The order channels are tried in for a model: the highest priority takes requests first. A lower priority is used only while every channel above it is unavailable; channels of one priority share requests by weight. The Usage choices (only provider, backup, share, prefer) set it for you. While supplies route requests, the call order on the Providers page orders channels instead, and new supplies of the channel start from its priority.

examples.effect: Tried before every channel at 0 that serves the same model in the same group.
The default. A backup at -1 is reached only while every channel at 0 fails.

settings.label: Weight
settings.description: How channels of the same priority share a model's requests: each takes its weight over the sum of the weights. Channels of other priorities are not counted. While supplies route requests, the supplies' own weights decide, and new supplies of the channel start from its weight.

examples.effect: Next to a channel of weight 1 at the same priority, takes about 3 / (3 + 1) = 75% of the requests.
The default: channels of one priority share requests equally.

settings.label: Cost ratio
settings.description: What the channel's upstream charges as a multiple of the catalog price, for channels without a price list. It is used only where the channel publishes no synced price: the channel cost is then catalog price x cost ratio x (1 + fee rate). It feeds the profit figures, the supply cost and the warning on user groups sold below it; users are never charged by it. Empty or 0 means unknown.

examples.effect: A relay at 80% of the official price: a $3 / $15 per million token model costs $2.40 / $12, or $2.52 / $12.60 with a 5% fee.
The upstream charges the official price; any group below ratio 1 is flagged as selling at a loss here.

settings.label: Fee rate
settings.description: What the channel's provider charges on top of its list prices, usually when you buy credit: cash paid / credit received - 1. A channel's cost is its list price x (1 + fee rate); costs decide which supply takes a request and which ones the price check holds. Recorded top-ups set it from the latest 10.

examples.effect: Requesty: $105 buys $100 of credit.
Vercel AI Gateway card payments: a $3.00 processing fee on $100 of credit.
An official vendor API billed at list price.

settings.label: Fee source
settings.description: Where the channel's fee rate comes from, such as a billing page or a checkout receipt. It is required once the fee rate is above 0. Only admins see it; users see a generic label.

settings.label: Groups
settings.description: The user groups the channel serves: a request is only sent to channels of the group it runs in. A request runs in its API key's group (then the key's backup group), or the user's group when the key has none. A channel needs at least one group.

examples.effect: Serves every user of the default group and keys set to it.
Serves both groups; each request is billed at the ratio of the group it ran in.

settings.label: Model mapping
settings.description: Renames on this channel only: a requested model name is sent upstream as another name. Use it only when the upstream wants its own names, such as deployment names; matching models to the catalog needs nothing here. A target starting with + bills by the requested name. Requests routed through a supply use the supply's upstream model instead. Saving a change rewrites the channel's model list to the requested names.

examples.effect: Requests for gpt-4o reach the upstream as my-gpt4o-deployment.
opus-latest is sent as claude-opus-4-1 and billed as opus-latest.

enum.label: Normal billing
enum.description: Count the input tokens, images included, before the request is sent.

enum.label: Exclude images
enum.description: Count the text only; images are left out of the estimate.

enum.label: Exclude all
enum.description: Count nothing beforehand; the reply's usage decides the charge.

settings.label: Pre-billing
settings.description: How the gateway counts a request's input before sending it, to hold the user's credit until the reply's usage is known. The count also stands in for the input when an upstream reports no usage, such as some streams. Leaving images or everything out saves server work on heavy requests; the prompt token limit is still checked.

settings.label: Models with streaming disabled
settings.description: Models this channel must not stream: streaming requests for them skip it for another channel serving the model. Requests without streaming still use it. Empty means every model streams.

examples.effect: Streaming requests for o1 and o1-pro go to other channels; plain requests still come here.

enum.label: Follow the site
enum.description: Inject when the site-wide Claude prompt caching switch is on.

enum.label: Always on
enum.description: Inject on this channel whatever the site switch says.

enum.label: Always off
enum.description: Never inject on this channel.

settings.label: Prompt caching injection
settings.description: Whether the gateway adds cache_control marks to Claude requests on this channel, so the upstream caches the prompt. Shown for Anthropic, Claude Code and OpenRouter channels, in the plugin settings. Requests that already carry cache_control are left alone. The plugin also sets the cache lifetime (5 minutes or 1 hour), where the marks go and which models match (Claude names by default).

settings.label: Proxy
settings.description: A proxy for this channel's upstream requests only, http or socks5. Only needed when this server cannot reach the upstream directly. A %s in the address is replaced with a session ID derived from the key, for proxies that pin one exit per session. Empty connects directly.

examples.effect: Every request of the channel goes through the local HTTP proxy.
Each key gets its own proxy session, so its exit address stays the same.

settings.label: Test model
settings.description: The model connection tests and scheduled checks send their request with. Empty picks a cheap chat model from the channel's list, else its first chat model; a channel without a chat model then cannot be tested.

examples.effect: Tests cost a fraction of a cent and do not touch the expensive models.

settings.label: Catalog price
settings.description: What the model costs before the group ratio, per million input and output tokens (or per request or minute). Users pay catalog price x their group ratio, whichever channel serves the request. It can be typed in USD, RMB or as a ratio (1 = $2 per million tokens). A model without a price is refused by default.

examples.effect: $3 input and $15 output per million tokens; the default group at 1.12 pays $3.36 / $16.80.
The same price as ratios: 1.5 x $2 = $3 and 7.5 x $2 = $15 per million tokens.

enum.label: Call order
enum.description: The supplies' priority and weight come from the call order on the Providers page.

enum.label: Set by hand
enum.description: The supplies keep the priority and weight stored on them.

settings.label: Supply order
settings.description: Whether the model's supplies follow the call order of the Providers page or keep their own numbers. Changing a supply's priority or weight on the Supplies tab sets the model to set by hand; switching back to the call order drops those numbers.

examples.effect: Moving a provider up on the Providers page moves it up for this model too.
This model keeps its order when the call order changes; new channels join below its supplies.

settings.default: the channel's priority; a supply added by hand joins below the lowest tier
settings.label: Priority
settings.description: This supply's tier among the model's supplies: higher tiers take requests first, lower ones back them up. A lower tier is used only while every supply above it is unavailable. Supplies of one priority form a tier and share it by weight. Under the call order the policy sets it; a supply with its own number no longer follows its channel.

examples.effect: Above two supplies at 1: they are used only while this supply fails.
Next to another supply at 1, the two form one tier and share its requests.

settings.label: Weight
settings.description: This supply's share of its tier: its weight over the tier's total. 0 counts as 1. Under the call order a provider's weight is split equally between its channels.

examples.effect: With a weight 1 supply in its tier: about 75% of the requests.
Two supplies of weight 1 share a tier 50 / 50. To keep a supply as a backup only, put it in the tier below.

settings.default: on; off for a supply an intake rule adds for review
settings.label: Use this supply
settings.description: Whether the supply takes the model's requests. Off, it keeps its settings but is skipped. Supplies an intake rule added wait switched off until you switch them on; switching a supply on also accepts its cost, so the price check leaves it alone.

settings.default: filled in from the channel's mapping, its model list or its platform's naming
settings.label: Upstream model
settings.description: The model name this supply sends to its channel's upstream. The client still asks for the public name and is billed by it; the channel's model mapping does not apply. A supply stops taking requests when the upstream stops listing this name in two checks in a row.

examples.effect: A Vertex channel serves the public claude-sonnet-4-5 under its own versioned name.
An aggregator that prefixes the vendor serves the same public model.

settings.default: created from the channels' priorities when supply routing starts
