settings.label: Call order
settings.description: The order channels take requests in while supplies route them, edited as the list on the Providers page. Each position is a provider (every channel of one type and address) or a single channel; positions shared by several split their requests by weight, and a provider's weight is split equally between its channels. Channels not placed come last, newest last. Models set by hand keep their own order.

examples.effect: The official Anthropic API first; channel 7 only while it fails.
Channels 3 and 5 share the first position: about 75% and 25% of the requests.

settings.label: Group ratio
settings.description: The multiplier on the catalog (official) price for users of the group: every request is charged catalog price x ratio, whatever channel serves it. The default group's ratio is the site's normal price and margin; other groups give discounts or charge more. 0 makes the group's requests free.

examples.effect: The default group sells at 12% over the official price: a $3 / $15 per million token model costs $3.36 / $16.80.
A VIP discount. With a 4% payment cost it brings in $1.008 per $1, below a 3% channel fee.
Sell at the official price: every channel fee and payment cost is a loss.

settings.label: API rate
settings.description: How many API requests each user of the group may send per minute, counted per user across all their keys. Requests over it get 429. Below 60 a fixed one-minute window counts them; from 60 a token bucket allows short bursts of up to 10 seconds' worth.

examples.effect: Five requests a second on average per user.
The 31st request within a minute is refused until the minute is over.

settings.label: Public
settings.description: Whether users outside the group may pick it for their API keys, as a key's group or backup group. Off, only users in the group use it. Requests through a picked group are billed at its ratio.

settings.label: Auto upgrade
settings.description: Moves users into this group when their total paid top-ups fall between its minimum and maximum. It is checked after each paid order; gifted credit (sign-up and invite bonuses, redemption codes, admin changes) does not count. When several groups match, the one with the highest minimum wins. A user an admin put in another group is moved too.

settings.label: Minimum paid top-ups
settings.description: The total paid top-ups from which auto upgrade moves a user into the group (inclusive). Only used with auto upgrade on.

examples.effect: With a maximum of 500: a user who has paid $100 up to $499.99 in total joins the group.
Every paying user matches, up to the maximum.

settings.label: Maximum paid top-ups
settings.description: The total paid top-ups at which the group stops matching (exclusive), so a bigger spender moves on to the next group. 0 means no upper bound. Only used with auto upgrade on.

examples.effect: A user reaching $500 in total moves to the group whose range starts at 500.
The top level: users stay however much they pay.

settings.label: Decision model
settings.description: The model that reads a session's first user message and picks one of the routes. A decision model is best: it answers with a probability for every label. A small, fast chat model also works. It is charged to the caller once per session, and it cannot be another routing policy.

examples.effect: A cheap chat model that returns logprobs, so the threshold is a real probability.

enum.label: Auto
enum.description: Logprobs where the channel returns them, else self-reported confidence for 24 hours.

enum.label: Logprobs only
enum.description: The label's real probability; requests fall back when logprobs are missing.

enum.label: Self-reported only
enum.description: The model answers its label and a confidence in JSON.

settings.label: Scoring
settings.description: How the decision model's confidence is measured before it is compared with the threshold. Logprobs need a non-reasoning model on a channel that returns them; Claude, reasoning models and most aggregators do not. A decision model ignores this setting.

settings.label: Confidence threshold
settings.description: The confidence the chosen route needs, from 0 to 1; below it the request goes to the fallback model. Raise it to send more borderline requests to the fallback, lower it to trust the decision model more. Self-reported confidence is only a ranking, so it compares less exactly than logprobs.

examples.effect: A message scored 62% coding / 38% writing goes to the coding route.
The same message goes to the fallback, since 62% is below 80%.
The top label always wins; only a failed decision uses the fallback.

settings.label: Fallback model
settings.description: Where a request goes when the confidence is below the threshold, the decision fails or the message has no text. A decision that times out counts as failed. Put your safest model here; it cannot be another routing policy.

examples.effect: Unclear and failed decisions get a strong general model rather than a cheap one.

settings.label: Pin per session
settings.description: How long a session keeps the model chosen at its first message. Later turns skip the decision, keep the upstream prompt cache warm and never switch models mid-conversation. 0 classifies every request; at most 7 days.

examples.effect: A conversation stays on its model for an hour after its first message, then is classified again.
Every request pays for a decision and may land on another model.

settings.label: Member limit
settings.description: The most members the organization may have, set by platform admins. It only stops new members from joining; existing members are not removed. Follow the site default, unlimited (0) or a number.

examples.effect: An organization with 20 members cannot invite or add a 21st until one leaves.
No limit, whatever the site default says.

settings.label: Approved models
settings.description: The most the organization may use, set by platform admins: every list of the organization stays inside it. Its default, members' lists and keys are all checked against the model actually called. A name ending in * allows a prefix, so new releases of a family follow; exact names need approving one by one. Empty means no limit.

examples.effect: Every Claude and GPT-5 model, including ones released later; nothing else.
Only that model; a request for any other model is refused.

settings.label: Default model access
settings.description: What members may use unless they have limits of their own, set by organization owners and admins. It is a named list or a list of models. Members with their own limits are not affected, and keys can only narrow what their creator may use. A name ending in * allows a prefix. Empty means every approved model.

examples.effect: Members use the cheap models only; a member given their own list can use more.

settings.label: Organization budget
settings.description: The most all members together may spend per day, week or month; then the organization's requests are refused. They are refused until the next period starts. Each member's own budget still applies. Periods start at midnight in the platform's reset time zone; changing the period restarts the count. None means no organization-wide cap.

examples.effect: When members have spent $1,000 in the month, every request of the organization is refused until the 1st.
A runaway script stops the team at $50 a day.

settings.label: Member budget
settings.description: The most one member may spend per day, week or month in the organization, set on the member's limits. Once used up, that member's requests are refused until the next period, while the organization budget caps everyone together. Keys the organization owns have no member budget. None means no cap of the member's own.

examples.effect: The member can spend $100 from Monday (or Sunday, per the site's week start) to the next week start.

enum.label: Keep for no key
enum.description: No organization key keeps its request and response bodies.

enum.label: Keep for every key
enum.description: Every organization key keeps its bodies, new keys included.

enum.label: Keep for selected keys
enum.description: Only the keys ticked in the list below keep their bodies; new keys start unticked.

settings.label: Request and response retention
settings.description: Which of the organization's API keys keep the bodies of their requests and responses. Only owners and admins set it, here: a key's creator cannot. Stored bodies never include API keys or auth headers, are deleted after 30 days, and only owners and platform admins can read them. Members are told on their keys who turned retention on and when. Shown only while the site allows retention.

examples.effect: Zero data retention for the whole organization.
An admin ticks the key of the app being debugged; the other keys keep nothing.

settings.label: Group
settings.description: The user group the key's requests run in: only channels of that group serve them, billed at its ratio. It must be the user's own group or a public one. Empty uses the user's group.

examples.effect: Requests use the vip channels and pay the vip ratio, even if the user is in default.

settings.label: Backup group
settings.description: A second group tried when the key's group has no channel that can take the request. A request served there is billed at the backup group's ratio and marked in the logs. With a group or backup group set, the user's own group is not tried.

examples.effect: Group vip with backup default: if every vip channel for the model fails, the request runs in default at its ratio.

settings.label: Model limits
settings.description: The models the key may call; others are refused. A name ending in * allows a prefix. With the switch on and no model selected, the key is not restricted. On an organization key it can only narrow what its creator may use, and may be a named list.

examples.effect: A key for a chatbot that can only reach the two cheap model families.

settings.label: Spending limit
settings.description: The most the key may spend; once used up, its requests are refused. With a reset period it is the limit per period instead. It only caps the key: the account balance always applies. Empty means no limit of the key's own.

examples.effect: Without a period, the key stops for good after $10 of usage.
The key can spend $5 a day; the count starts over at midnight.

enum.label: Daily
enum.description: Starts over at midnight.

enum.label: Weekly
enum.description: Starts over at midnight on the first day of the week.

enum.label: Monthly
enum.description: Starts over at midnight on the 1st.

settings.label: Reset period
settings.description: How often the key's spending limit starts over. Without a period the limit is spent once. Periods start at midnight in the platform's reset time zone, weeks on its week start; changing the period restarts the count. A period needs a limit above 0.
